prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

Beyond the practical limitation, there is also the conceptual ”elephant in the room” limitation that we do not know if neural networks would suffer in a way analogous to humans. === key 8cb0d0f86c21
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Whether suffering would be more likely to arise in language models or RL agents
Write-up text before the decision: hus, GPT-n could have 10^20 parameters and still not suffer, or a much smaller network could already show suffering for other reasons. **Why would they suffer?** Suffering is not just a random feature of the universe but likely has a specific evolutionary advantage. In animals, the core objective is to advance their genes to the next generation. Since the world is complex and the rewards for procreation are sparse and might be far into the future, the ability to suffer evolved as a proxy to maximize the propagation of genes. Suffering thus reduces the complexity of the world and sparsity of the reward to very immediate feedback, e.g. avoid danger or stay in social communities, because they are long-term predictors of the ultimate goal of reproduction. Similarly, consciousness could have arisen to make better decisions in a complex world and then spiraled out of control, as our conscious goals are not aligned anymore with the original goal of reproduction. This misalignment between an inner and an outer optimization procedure has been coined mesa-optimization ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01820), [AF post](/tag/mesa-optimization), [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bJLcIBixGj8&ab_channel=RobertMiles)). It yields a possible explanation for when suffering could arise even when the user does not intend it. Thus, we argue that the probability of NN suffering is increased by a) higher complexity of the environment since suffering is a heuristic to avoid bad circumstances and b) sparser rewards since dense rewards require fewer proxies and heuristics. === key bedb5da45f13
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to state the empirical confirmation of the theory
Write-up text before the decision: we want to explore in the following. We compare the small CNN and the linear network that were already used before with a network we call OneNet (code in appendix). OneNet has only one input neuron and a larger second and third layer. Thus, the ratio between the first and other layers is very small and we can see that the theoretical maximum for the backward-forward ratio of 3:1 can be observed in practice. Furthermore, we look at exponentially increasing batch sizes for all three architectures. In the case of linear networks, i.e. LinearNet and OneNet, the ratio decreases with increasing batch size since the influence of the weight update is reduced. In the case of the CNN, the FLOP count is completely dominated by layers and the weight update is negligible. This effect is so strong that no change can be observed in the figure. We see that LinearNet converges to a backward-forward ratio of 1:1 for larger batch sizes while OneNet converges to 2:1.
